Curie Temperature

The Curie temperature Tc of heat-treated samples increases with the increase of Fe content

(Fig. 11). Besides the fact that larger magnetic moment is introduced by the Co → Fe substitution,

this is also accompanied by the lattice expansion (mostly along c-axis, which is the easy axis) (Fig.

4a), increasing the ferromagnetic exchange interaction [52].

There are also changes in the shape of the magneto-gravimetric curves with increasing Fe

content (Fig. 11). Two ferromagnetic transitions are clearly noticeable on plots of first derivatives

of the effective weight versus the temperature (Fig. 12). The low-temperature Tc1 and the high-

temperature Tc2, are visible in all samples, except x = 0. In the sample x = 0.20 with highest Fe

content and clearly contain a second phase, those two peaks are separated the most.

This is also in accord with the composite nature of the material and the idea that with

increasing Fe content the system becomes less stable. However, it is difficult to explain the

presence of high-temperature Tc2 by the presence of the 2:7-type intercalations, because the

2:7 phase is known to be weakly ferromagnetic with a very low transition point of 50 K [53]. One

possibility is it’s compositionally far from the standard 2:7 compound.

## Discussion

The microstructural characterization clearly shows that the composition range explored has

a region of solubility 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.19 for formation of the CaCu5-type structure (Fig. 8). This is based

on both, stabilization of lattice dimensions (predominantly a and V) and clearly two phases in the

last sample with x = 0.20 (Fig. 2d). The EDS analysis detects clear presence of the 2:7 phase, often

with small epitaxial inclusions of 5:19 and/or 1:3 phases within the precipitate. Annealing below

840 °C shows the development of the stacking faults. SEM and XRD indicate that these stacking

faults become more prevalent for heat-treated samples with x > 0.13. Increased Bragg peak

broadening suggests there is strain associated with the basal plane stacking faults uniformly

distributed within the matrix (Fig. 4b). TEM data shows that these stacking faults are coherent

with the matrix and coarsen with increasing x, occasionally segregated into extended basal plane

2:7/5:19-type intercalated regions. The strain reaches the maximum at x = 0.19, further Fe content

causes the system to transform into the multi-phase material, rather than forming a uniform

composite, releasing the interfacial strain caused by the stacking faults and/or their extended

intercalated regions. The data supports the solubility range narrowing with decreasing temperature


<!-- Page 12 -->


and the excess solutes are accommodated by forming coherent basal plane stacking faults. The

annealing experiments suggest that the decompositions of the solid solution is kinetically limited

with a preference for the Ce-rich and Fe-, Cu-depleted second phase to form coherent

2:7/5:19-type intercalations and/or precipitates.

The ubiquitous stacking faults in the material form a laminar structure, with the irregular

spacing along [0001] which coincides with easy magnetization axis of the matrix. The strictly

anisotropic nature of the faults and very irregular matrix fragmentation are two main

microstructural features that define the magnetic behavior of the material and help to explain the

magnetization as well as the coercivity data of the as-cast and heat-treated samples, (Fig.10 upper-

left and lower-right inset). In the as-cast material, the presence of any defects is minimal, thus the

magnetization increases gradually with the increase of the Fe content (Fig. 10 upper-left inset),

while the coercivity is minimal and stable within ~ 300 – 500 Oe. For the heat-treated samples

various local structures that combine 1:5 matrix slabs and 1:2 insertions similar as those depicted

in Fig. 8 form along the c axis. We speculate that these then cause the spatial variation of anisotropy

field. They introduce strain and compositional irregularity into main hard magnetic matrix

material, serve as nucleation and/or curling points for reversal domains. Depending on their

distribution within the matrix the pinning mechanism changes. Regular nano-distribution of the

secondary 2:7/5:19 phase, in form of stacking faults, creates the composite, strictly anisotropic

sub-grain structure with domain wall nucleation regulated mainly by anisotropy fluctuations. This

allows sustained magnetization within the whole substitution range and as well as stable

coercivities which are primarily defined by magnetocrystalline anisotropy. For x = 0.2, the

segregation of the secondary phase into the micron sized 2:7/5:19 precipitates causes significant

drop in magnetization because of decreased volume fraction of the main magnetic phase as well

as increased coercivity due to introduction of physical obstacles that can pin domain wall in a hard

manner.

While the presence of the second phases is below the detectability limit for XRD, the M-

TGA data clearly shows two distinct magnetic transitions for x > 0.15 (Fig 12). One possible

explanation of high Tc2 may be related to matrix degradation during the heat treatment so that the

certain fraction of Ce- and/or Cu-depleted component, for example, 1:7 and/or 2:17, evolves with

Tc higher than the matrix. It is known that the 1:5 phases decompose at low temperatures by a

eutectoid transformation 1:5 → 2:7 + 2:17 [54]. It is also known that the 1:5 Ce/Co/Cu undergoes


<!-- Page 13 -->


spinodal-like transformation below 800 oC [55] through the formation of Cu-rich and Cu-poor

coherent components. In both cases, there is a chance for appearance of additional Ce- and/or Cu-

depleted phase with high Curie temperatures. In addition to the defects, how does the changes in

the chemistry alter the matrix: (i) – very local compositional variations in the matrix apart from

the stacking faults and/or precipitates, or (ii) – compositional variations that occur because of these

local features. We clearly state that we do not observe the first scenario (Fig. S1 – 3). However,

the second scenario is not excluded and is realized through the variable frequency of the defects.

In places/volumes with dense array of stacking faults the surrounding matrix must be slightly Ce

and Co depleted in comparison to the matrix with rare stacking faults. As discussed above, the

existence of the second Curie point Tc2 is most likely related to the distribution of the defects.

When the density is low and their width is very fine, ~ a few nm in thickness Tc2 is less detectable

from the direct magneto-gravimetric curves. With increasing Fe and after heat treatment, the larger

number of, and thicker these extended intercalated regions become, M-TGA clearly shows two

Curie points as discussed above (Fig. 11, 12). The fact that the Tc1 and the lattice volume both

increase in a fairly smooth rate with increasing x is indicative that the matrix properties are

dominated only by the substitution of Fe for Co. The trend in the number and size of the extended

intercalated regions with increasing Fe, as evidenced by the SEM/TEM, the increase of the strained

lattice as well as the M-TGA all point to these Ce rich, 2:7/5:19 like regions are the Tc2 phase.

We speculate that the strain improves the energy density of the system. Typically, additional

Fe reduces the magnetocrystalline anisotropy. We observe such trend in the as-cast samples with x

= 0.13 (107 kOe) and x = 0.19 (89 kOe), respectively. However after the heat treatment the

difference between the two is minimal, i.e., 110 kOe for x = 0.13 and 112 kOe for x = 0.19. The

post annealing energy density improvement for x = 0.19 is eight times higher than in Fe-poor

x = 0.13 (Fig. 10).

The material is coarse-grained with grain size up to 300 – 500 μm. We also show that the

‘phase separation’ within these individual large grains is very anisotropic due to the nature of these

coherent, basal-plane stacking faults and their more extended intercalated regions with higher Fe

content. The resulting segmented regions that develop during the magnetic hardening strictly

follows the “parent” grain’s crystallographic orientation.  For the grain-aligned samples, this

behavior results in a hysteresis loop of coherently rotating single SW-particle (Stoner-Wohlfarth)

[56] similar to that of fully optimized best commercial magnet [57], especially in cases with


<!-- Page 14 -->


x = 0.13 – 0.17 (Fig. 9). The key here may lie in the large grain size. If in fact the formation of the

extended intercalated regions are kinetically limited at the low annealing temperatures, much finer

grain sizes may result in formation of distinct second phases.

To elucidate this, we turned to similar works [58 – 65] on domain-wall pinning in Sm-Co

magnets. A recent study [58] explicitly explains the domain reversal mechanism in 2:17-type Sm-

Co magnet. Although this system is different, some structural features are very similar to the 2-17

compound. The Sm-Co magnet has typical cellular microstructure with softer 2:17-type matrix

and harder 1:5-type pyramidal-like cell edges. There is also a so-called Z-phase that is linear

(planar and/or platelet-like) and continuously crosses the cells. These lines are strictly

perpendicular to easy axis ,i.e., c-axis, similar to our observations. According to reference [58], the

Z-phase is where the reverse domains originate. The proposed reversal mechanism is curling of

the moments away from the easy axis and occurs inside of Z-phase.

The nucleated domains freely propagate within the cell until impeded by hard magnetic

1:5-type cell boundaries. This would imply the linear defects are the places where curling starts.

Similar structural features like Z-phase are observed also in our phase, i.e., the 2:7-type

defects. Compositionally these structural features might be slightly different, but functionally they

play similar role: they are the places where the anisotropy fluctuation occurs both in anisotropy

energy as well as in direction.

The geometry of the domains can be described as 360o cloud-like shape. This implies that

there exists strong magnetic exchange coupling interaction and spontaneous magnetization, which

causes the directions of local magnetic moments to turn towards the hard phase and then be aligned

to the same direction. If the exchange energy is high then it is difficult to do any non-uniform

rotation of magnetization. This results in large size domains, so-called interaction domains [66]

within the large “parent” grain. This is possible if the material does not have a constantly strong

and regular magneto-crystalline anisotropy. The magnetocrystalline anisotropy is distributed

unevenly and depends on the local atomic order, which subsequently depends on the initial phase

decomposition and coexistence of CaCu5-related structural motifs.

The domain wall is not pinned as in Sm-Co, because there are no cells and no cell

boundaries of a hard magnetic phase.  However, the wall propagation is not completely free of

resistance since the stacking defects serve as physical obstacles to the extent which depends on

their thickness.  Unlike the zig-zag domain wall front in the Z-phase [58], the boundary is smoother


<!-- Page 15 -->


because of local anisotropy fluctuations. As a result, the coercivity is mainly driven by nucleation

rather than domain wall pinning in the samples with square hysteresis loops, e.g., as in x = 0.19.

However, in x = 0.20 the reversal mechanism must include significant pinning component, because

the re-magnetization requires significantly larger fields than the critical field (Fig 9, green loop).

Thus, the coercivity in Ce(Co1-xFex)4.4Cu0.6 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.19) is dictated by regularity of the

defects which become nano-distributed within the matrix without the formation of large

aggregates.  The domain reversal in this case is very coherent since all defects are perfectly

oriented along [0001], which means that all the formed “sub-grains” are ideally field-aligned for

single-grained particles. As larger aggregates of the 2:7 phase form the volume fraction of low-

magnetization phase increases, increasing the number of pinning sites. Thus, the coercivity starts

depending more on domain wall pinning rather than nucleation.

## Conclusions

The series of Ce(Co1-xFex)4.4Cu0.6 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.19) compositions was systematically

investigated to understand the role of chemistry and processing on their magnetic properties. The

series, which forms a solid solution at high temperatures, undergoes a phase decomposition below

~840°C for samples with x ≥ 0.13 due to narrowing of the solubility limit. Annealing at 400°C

transforms these compounds into a composite magnet that consists of 1:5-type matrix with basal

plane 2:7/5:19-type coherent extended intercalated regions which increase in their number and

thickness with increasing Fe form a coherent laminated nanostructure. The limited formation of

these coherent secondary phases at these lower annealing temperatures is most likely due to limited

diffusivity and structural similarity to other metastable phases in the Sm-Co family of compounds.

The overall increase in the saturation magnetization and Curie temperature is due to Fe substitution

for Co while the increase in coercivity is depend on the spatial dispersal of the stacking faults and

their extended intercalated regions. The distribution of the nano-scale intercalations and the

1:5-type matrix forms a composite, anisotropic sub-grain structure within the single grain particles

that behave as single SW particles. The magnetization data is consistent with domain wall

nucleation regulated mainly by anisotropy fluctuations. Segregation of the basal plane extended

intercalated regions adds physical obstacles that pin domain walls. The coherent 2:7-type regions

serve as nucleation places rather than hard pining sites. However, their irregular spacing causes


<!-- Page 16 -->


fluctuation of the magnetocrystalline anisotropy which subsequently strengthens magnetic

exchange interactions and leads to the formation of large irregular interaction domains.

Temperature performance and optimizations The reversible temperature coefficients (RTC) for magnetic remanence α = (Br(0) – Br(127)- Br(0)*127)*100 (α = -0.13 %/oC) and coercivity β = (Hc(0) – Hc(127)-Br(0)*127)*100 (β = -0.21

%/oC) were determined for x = 0.15 within the temperature range 0 – 127

oC, (Fig. S.4). In comparison to the commercial magnets it falls in the range between SmCo and NdFeB [57]. Thermal optimization includes two experiments: (i) - variation of maximum (solutionizing) temperature and (ii) – variation of minimum (hardening) temperature (Fig. S.5). All other parameters including times and rates remain the same, i.e., 10h solutionizing, 6h hardening and 10 oC/min cooling rate. The effect of decreased solutionizing temperature as well as effect of increased hardening temperature is studied with respect to microstructure and magnetic properties. X-ray analysis shows that the material always remains as predominantly 1:5 phase (Fig S.6 a). No significant change in lattice parameters is detected. The SEM examination of solutionizing temperature variation samples shows uniform surface at 940 oC, then stripe-like distribution of 1:5 and 2:7 at 840 oC. Most significant difference of microstructure occurs at 740 oC, where the 2:7 component is segregated into large globular features (Fig S.6 c). Decrease of solutionizing temperature causes increase of coercivity and decrease of magnetization (Fig. 7 a,c). The shape of the hysteresis loop becomes less rectangular which indicates on change in pinning mechanism (Fig. S.7a). Field much stronger than the critical is required re-magnetize the material, i.e., in quadrant 3 and 4, which means that domain walls are strongly pinned. The volume fraction of magnetic matrix is decreased since the magnetization drops by ~15 – 17 %. All the experiments evidently indicate that system becomes increasingly phase-separated as the maximum temperature decreases. It starts magnetically behave similar to the maximum Fe-content sample, x = 0.20 (Fig.9). At 740 oC the system is less kinetically restricted, the stacking faults segregate into thick weakly magnetic 2:7 intercalated regions and/or precipitates. This in-turn is immediately reflected on magnetic properties, i.e., drop of magnetization because of decreased fraction of magnetic phase, and increase in coercivity because of additional precipitation pining. In the samples with hardening temperature variations there is no drastic change of X-ray patterns and microstructure (Fig S.6b,d). The only detectable difference is in stripe-like rare segregates of 2:7 phase precipitates at 600 and 800 oC. Increase of the hardening temperature does not significantly change the shape of the hysteresis loops (Fig. S.7b). They remain very rectangular and re-magnetization runs easy.  This means that the pinning mechanism does not change much. However, the coercivity decrease indicates that less energy is required for reverse domain nucleation. The structure of the material should be more defective as the hardening temperature increases. However, these defects are small in size and uniformly spread throughout the matrix so that they serve as a nucleation sites rather than domain wall pinning. The optimization experiments show that the standard heat treatment procedure is close to optimum. One advantage would be in decrease of the solutionizing temperature by 80 – 100 oC. This does not bring significant losses in both magnetization and coercivity, but significant portion of energy can be spared.  Another important aspect of thermal optimization is variation of cooling rates. This work is in progress and will be reported shortly.
